blocks.content: kubectl top shows real-time CPU and memory usage for nodes or Pods, a quick, direct view that depends entirely on the Metrics Server covered in the Autoscaling module.
kubectl top gives you a live, current snapshot of actual CPU and memory consumption, immediately useful for spotting a Pod or node under unexpected load, right now.

blocks.alt: A live, current snapshot, not historical trends or averages

blocks.content: 2. A Direct Dependency on Metrics Server
blocks.text: 2. A Direct Dependency on Metrics Server

blocks.content: This is worth stating explicitly, exactly as covered in the Autoscaling module's Metrics Server topic, this command has no data to show at all if Metrics Server is not installed and running, it reads from that exact same source the HPA relies on.

blocks.alt: The same required dependency covered explicitly in the Autoscaling module

blocks.content:
kubectl top nodes
# NAME     CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
# node-1   450m         22%    3200Mi          40%

code.content:
kubectl top nodes
# NAME     CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
# node-1   450m         22%    3200Mi          40%

codes.bash:
kubectl top nodes
# NAME     CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
# node-1   450m         22%    3200Mi          40%

blocks.content: kubectl top nodes gives a cluster-wide view, how much of each node's capacity is actually in use, kubectl top pods narrows in on specific workloads, showing exactly which Pods are consuming the most.

blocks.alt: A cluster-wide view, or a workload-specific one, depending on what you need

blocks.content:
kubectl top pods
# NAME              CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# my-app-7d9f8c      120m         256Mi

code.content:
kubectl top pods
# NAME              CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# my-app-7d9f8c      120m         256Mi

codes.bash:
kubectl top pods
# NAME              CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# my-app-7d9f8c      120m         256Mi

blocks.content: Quickly checking whether a specific Pod is approaching its resource limit (covered in the Namespaces & Resource Management module), before it gets throttled or OOMKilled, is a common, practical reason to reach for this command directly.

blocks.alt: A quick, direct check, before a resource limit becomes an actual problem

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl top shows live CPU and memory usage for nodes or Pods, but it has a hard dependency on Metrics Server being installed and running.
top nodes gives a cluster-wide capacity view, top pods narrows in on specific workload consumption, both draw from the exact same underlying data source.
